reason: Start building the red-cell component needed to carry oxygen.
expectation: The developing cells will make haemoglobin, though I am unsure whether they will also mature in this step.

alternatives.reason: Making plasma would also advance blood assembly, but I want to start with oxygen transport.

effect: The cells matured as well as assembling haemoglobin, so I can now examine oxygen binding.
reaction: The developing-cell inset usefully connects protein production to the mature, nucleus-free discs.
reason: Test oxygen binding in the newly made red blood cells.
expectation: Oxygen will bind to haemoglobin; I am unsure whether this step will also show its release.

alternatives.reason: Plasma is needed for blood assembly, but oxygen binding follows directly from the red-cell construction.

effect: The double arrow and explanation show both binding and release, completing the oxygen-binding goal; blood assembly remains.
reaction: The link between low dissolved oxygen in tissues and oxygen release is useful.
reason: Make plasma for the remaining blood-assembly goal; this is the only offered combination.
expectation: Water and solutes will form plasma, ready to combine with blood cells.

effect: Plasma is ready to receive the cellular components needed for blood assembly.
reaction: The straw-yellow fluid and dissolved proteins make the plasma component clear.
reason: Add the white cells and platelets to build up the blood's cellular components.
expectation: Plasma will contain white cells and platelets, with red cells still to be added.

alternatives.reason: Adding oxygen-bearing red cells would also advance assembly, but either order seems plausible.

effect: The plasma now contains white cells and platelets; adding red cells remains.
reaction: The picture clearly distinguishes the larger white cells from platelet fragments.
reason: Add the red cells to complete blood assembly; this is the only offered combination.
expectation: The combination will produce blood containing plasma, red and white cells, and platelets.

effect: Adding red cells completed the blood model and the remaining goal, bringing its fluid and cellular components together.
reaction: The final picture clearly distinguishes the components, though it says little about the roles of white cells and platelets.

mostWorthwhile.text: Showing haemoglobin binding and releasing oxygen was most worthwhile: the double arrow and low-oxygen tissue explanation connect a molecular interaction to transport.

leastWorthwhile.text: Making plasma was relatively predictable, and its picture added little beyond the listed water and solutes.

surprise.text: The first combination showed maturation into nucleus-free red cells as well as haemoglobin assembly; I had not been sure it would do both.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though adding white cells and platelets together was a straightforward assembly step rather than an explanation of their distinct functions.

continue.text: I would probably continue to see how circulation brings oxygen carriers close to tissues; this chapter establishes binding and release but leaves that connection for later.
